meta.corpus: The Federalist Papers (32 single-author papers), see data/manifest.json
meta.status: DRAFT written with AI assistance BEFORE any retrieval run; the student must read, edit and take ownership of every question.
meta.split_method: Fixed before experiments. Test questions come from papers that no dev question uses (fed09 is not used; test = fed31, fed64, fed65, fed72, fed78). Questions are English because the corpus is English.
meta.leak_risk: Dev and test are in different papers, but dev d05/d08 (separation of powers) and test t01 (judiciary) are topically close; fed65/fed72 (executive/Senate powers) are close to dev d09/d10. Treat test numbers as indicative only (n=5).
meta.filter_note: A 'filter' is the author scope supplied by the user/context BEFORE retrieval (e.g. 'only Madison's essays'). The question text never names the author, the gold paper or the answer. Strategy C applies the filter; A and B ignore it.
meta.selection_criteria: Fixed before running retrieval: choose by Evidence Hit@3 on DEV; ties broken by Hit@1 on DEV, then by manual grounding score, then by resources (chunk count, embed time). The TEST split is run once, only after the choice is frozen (python -m src.run eval --split test --final).
meta.selection_criteria_amendment: 2026-11-13, after the DEV run (test not run): the tie-breaker 'manual grounding score' cannot be used before the test run because grounding is labelled on the test split. Amended tie-breakers, using dev/non-test information only: 1) Evidence Hit@3 on dev, 2) Hit@1 on dev, 3) fewer chunks / lower embed time, 4) simpler setup (no filter needed from the user). The change was made after seeing dev results, which tie B and C; it does not use any test information.
meta.frozen_decision: 2026-11-13, BEFORE the test run: the student reviewed all 20 questions and the corpus and chose strategy B (paragraph chunks, no filter). Dev result unchanged after review (A 9/15 and 12/15; B 11/15 and 14/15; C 11/15 and 14/15). B and C tie on dev; B was preferred because it needs no user-supplied filter. A, B and C are all reported on test; the choice is not changed after seeing test.
meta.evidence_rule: evidence_quote is verbatim (whitespace/case-insensitive) from the gold unit of the normalized corpus; verified by python -m src.verify_benchmark.

questions.question: How is a faction defined?
questions.expected_answer: A group of citizens, a majority or a minority, united by a common impulse of passion or interest that is adverse to the rights of other citizens or the community's permanent interests.
questions.evidence_quote: united and actuated by some common impulse of passion, or of interest, adversed to the rights of other citizens

questions.question: What is named as the most common and lasting source of factions?
questions.expected_answer: The various and unequal distribution of property.
questions.evidence_quote: the most common and durable source of factions has been the various and unequal distribution of property

questions.question: In what two ways does a republic differ from a pure democracy?
questions.expected_answer: Government is delegated to a small number of elected citizens, and a republic can extend over a greater number of citizens and a greater sphere of country.
questions.evidence_quote: the delegation of the government, in the latter, to a small number of citizens elected by the rest; secondly, the greater number of citizens, and greater sphere of country

questions.question: If government is administered by men over men, what must it first be enabled to do and what must it then be obliged to do?
questions.expected_answer: First enable the government to control the governed, and then oblige it to control itself.
questions.evidence_quote: you must first enable the government to control the governed; and in the next place oblige it to control itself

questions.question: What arrangement of power is described as the very definition of tyranny?
questions.expected_answer: The accumulation of all legislative, executive and judiciary powers in the same hands.
questions.evidence_quote: may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny

questions.question: How can a republic be defined in terms of where its powers come from?
questions.expected_answer: A government that derives all its powers directly or indirectly from the great body of the people.
questions.evidence_quote: a government which derives all its powers directly or indirectly from the great body of the people

questions.question: How do the powers given to the federal government compare with those left to the State governments?
questions.expected_answer: Federal powers are few and defined; those remaining with the States are numerous and indefinite.
questions.evidence_quote: are few and defined. Those which are to remain in the State governments are numerous and indefinite

questions.question: Why are written limits on each department of government not a sufficient defense against encroachment?
questions.expected_answer: Experience shows such paper limits are overrated as protection against the encroaching spirit of power.
questions.evidence_quote: parchment barriers against the encroaching spirit of power

questions.question: What does giving every State an equal vote in the upper chamber recognize?
questions.expected_answer: It is a constitutional recognition of the portion of sovereignty remaining in the individual States, and an instrument for preserving it.
questions.evidence_quote: the equal vote allowed to each State is at once a constitutional recognition of the portion of sovereignty remaining in the individual States

questions.question: What does the method of choosing the President guarantee about the person who holds that office?
questions.expected_answer: A moral certainty that the office will not fall to anyone who is not eminently endowed with the requisite qualifications.
questions.evidence_quote: affords a moral certainty, that the office of President will never fall to the lot of any man who is not in an eminent degree endowed with the requisite qualifications

questions.question: What do the people of the country have in common in terms of ancestry, language and religion?
questions.expected_answer: They are descended from the same ancestors, speak the same language and profess the same religion.
questions.evidence_quote: descended from the same ancestors, speaking the same language, professing the same religion

questions.question: What fundamental question is posed about whether societies can establish good government by choice rather than by accident and force?
questions.expected_answer: Whether societies of men are really capable of establishing good government from reflection and choice, or are forever destined to depend on accident and force.
questions.evidence_quote: forever destined to depend for their political constitutions on accident and force

questions.question: Why was government instituted in the first place?
questions.expected_answer: Because the passions of men will not conform to reason and justice without constraint.
questions.evidence_quote: Because the passions of men will not conform to the dictates of reason and justice, without constraint

questions.question: What are the principal purposes the union is meant to serve?
questions.expected_answer: Common defense, preservation of public peace against internal and external attacks, regulation of commerce, and the conduct of foreign intercourse.
questions.evidence_quote: the common defense of the members; the preservation of the public peace as well against internal convulsions as external attacks

questions.question: In what sense is the Constitution itself said to be a bill of rights?
questions.expected_answer: In every rational sense and to every useful purpose the Constitution is itself a bill of rights.
questions.evidence_quote: in every rational sense, and to every useful purpose, A BILL OF RIGHTS

questions.question: Why is the judicial branch described as having neither the sword nor the purse?
questions.expected_answer: It has neither force nor will, only judgment, and depends on the executive arm for the efficacy of its judgments.
questions.evidence_quote: neither FORCE nor WILL, but merely judgment

questions.question: What kind of offenses fall within the jurisdiction of impeachment?
questions.expected_answer: Offenses that proceed from the misconduct of public men, the abuse or violation of some public trust.
questions.evidence_quote: those offenses which proceed from the misconduct of public men

questions.question: Why is it necessary to let the people continue an officer in his station when they approve of his conduct?
questions.expected_answer: Re-eligibility enables the people, when they see reason to approve of an officer's conduct, to continue him in his station.
questions.evidence_quote: to enable the people, when they see reason to approve of his conduct, to continue him in his station

questions.question: What precautions should surround the power of making treaties?
questions.expected_answer: It should be delegated only in a mode that gives the highest security that it will be exercised by the best qualified men.
questions.evidence_quote: it should not be delegated but in such a mode, and with such precautions, as will afford the highest security that it will be exercised by men the best qualified for the purpose

questions.question: What kind of truths do all subsequent reasoning in any field of inquiry depend on?
questions.expected_answer: Certain primary truths, or first principles.
questions.evidence_quote: certain primary truths, or first principles, upon which all subsequent reasonings must depend
